newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU delay option not seen included in Maastricht.
newsitem.headline: EMU delay option not seen included in Maastricht.

text.p: The idea that the Maastricht Treaty gives European Union leaders the option to set a different start date for monetary union than 1999 misinterprets a clause designed to allow an earlier launch, EU officials say.
Specifically, proponents of a delay to economic and monetary union (EMU) argue that the EU could avoid a contentious renegotiation of Maastricht by simply invoking the option set out in Article 109J.
The oft-quoted clause states that "if by the end of 1997 the date for the beginning of the third stage has not been set, the third stage shall start on 1 January 1999."
What some have interpreted this to mean is that another date beyond 1999 could be agreed among EU countries before the end of this year.
The dominant view among EU monetary officials is that such an interpretation neglects a proper reading of the treaty and is therefore not valid.
"In effect this is not a loophole," said one senior EU official.
"It's not possible because in order to do this before the end of 1997 a majority of member states need to be ready and that is clearly not the case," he added.

In fact, at the end of last year EU finance ministers had to formally decide that a majority of countries were not ready to join EMU ahead of 1999. Their decision has eliminated the option of setting a later date.
More importantly, say officials, the clause was actually intended to allow an earlier start date, not one beyond 1999.
Along with the "empty shell" scenario, which has EMU starting on paper but with no members, EU officials say the only conceivable way of delaying EMU is to revisit the treaty.
Several have advanced the possibility of a short technical delay -- six months, for example -- to ensure that the European Central Bank is fully operational.
But if a delay is needed to allow countries like Germany extra time to meet the convergence criteria, one would have to have a treaty renegotiation, they added.
Most believe it is premature to make such a judgement, with the earliest possible time seen later in the year when the economic situation in Europe becomes clearer.

Still others, such as Bundesbank Council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, argue that it will become apparent in May that Germany will miss the treaty's deficit criterion without additional spending cuts.
Countries wishing to qualify for EMU must bring their 1997 budget deficits down to three percent of total output.
